## Abstract

The glandular stomach is comprised of two regenerative compartments termed corpus and antrum, and our understanding of the transcriptional networks that maintain these tissues is incomplete. Here, we show that cell types with equivalent functional roles in the corpus and antrum share similar transcriptional states including the poorly characterized stem cells of the isthmus region. To further study the isthmus, we developed a monolayer (2D) culture system that is continually maintained by Wnt-responsive isthmus-like cells capable of differentiating into several gastric cell types. Importantly, 2D cultures can be converted into conventional 3D organoids, modeling the plasticity of gastric epithelial cells in vivo. Finally, we utilized the 2D culture system to show that Sox2 is both necessary and sufficient to generate enterochromaffin (EC) cells. Together, our data provide important insights into gastric homeostasis, establish a tractable culture system to capture isthmus cells, and uncover a role for Sox2 in EC cells.

## Introduction

The glandular stomach forms a repeated series of epithelial glands that contain highly specialized cells responsible for barrier formation, digestion, nutrient sensing, and hormone production. Certain gastric cell types such as mucus-producing pit cells are present throughout the stomach epithelium, while other cell types are enriched in one of the two major glandular compartments commonly referred to as the corpus and antrum1,2. For example, corpus glands in the proximal stomach are enriched for acid-producing parietal cells and pepsinogen-producing chief cells. By contrast, antral glands in the distal stomach are enriched for hormone-producing enteroendocrine (EE) cells.

Classical label-retention experiments have suggested that differentiated cells of the corpus and antrum are continuously replenished by multipotent stem cells that reside within a centrally located, proliferative region of the gastric gland termed the isthmus3,4. Subsequent genetic lineage tracing experiments using promoter-driven Cre alleles5–11 have confirmed the existence of constitutive (i.e. homeostatic) stem cell populations within this niche (Extended Data Fig. 1a). Parallel studies using alternative Cre drivers have identified multipotent cells in a distinct region called the gland base11–13. Of note, gland base cells in the antrum contain immature cells that function as constitutive stem cells while gland base cells in the corpus contain mature chief cells that function as facultative (i.e. injury-dependent) stem cells11,14–16. Similarly, differentiated parietal cells17, tuft cells18 and unidentified Villin-expressing cells19 have been suggested to function as facultative stem cells capable of repopulating entire gastric units in certain contexts. To molecularly characterize gastric epithelial cells during development, homeostasis and malignant transformation, recent studies have employed single cell RNA-Sequencing9,20–23, providing a valuable initial framework for comparing and contrasting specific gastric cell types across different contexts. However, we still lack a complete understanding of how the various immature and mature gastric epithelial cell populations of the corpus and antrum, particularly isthmus and gland base cells, are related to one another.

The ability to explant and expand various stem cells in vitro has been instrumental to study the biology of several regenerative tissues. In the stomach, early studies reported the successful explantation of mouse and human gastric epithelial cells, although these cultures could not be maintained long-term24–28. Seminal follow-up studies demonstrated that embedding gastric glands in Matrigel facilitates the indefinite expansion of epithelial cells as three-dimensional (3D) organoids, which require Lgr5-expressing gland base-like cells to maintain the cuture13,29–33. By contrast, isthmus stem cells have not yet been definitively identified in 3D cultures, thus making a direct comparison between gland base and isthmus stem cells challenging. It is therefore critical to develop additional, tractable culture methods that reflect the diversity of gastric epithelial homeostasis and capture both isthmus and gland base cells.

## Results

### Epithelial diversity within the glandular stomach

To establish unbiased transcriptional maps of gastric epithelial cells from the corpus and antrum, we performed single cell RNA-Sequencing34 of dissociated and sorted Epcampos/AnnexinVneg cells from both compartments (Fig. 1a). We assigned specific cell types using previously described markers in combination with differential gene expression patterns (Fig. 1b). Cell types common to both the corpus and antrum included mucus-producing pit cells (Muc5ac+), which reside at the top of the glandular units; mucus-producing gland base/neck cells (Muc6+), which reside in the gland base of the antrum or the analogous neck region of the corpus; and proliferating cells (Mki67+) in the centrally located isthmus (Fig. 1c,d). Additionally, we identified enteroendocrine (EE) cells (Chga+/Chgb+) and tuft cells (Dclk1+), which are scattered throughout antral and corpus glands (Fig. 1c,d). By contrast, we detected chief cells (Gif+) and parietal cells (Atp4a+) specifically in the corpus consistent with their presence in the gland base and neck of the corpus, respectively (Fig. 1c). Within the EE cell lineage, we could further distinguish the five previously identified cellular subtypes including serotonin-producing enterochromaffin (EC) cells (Tph1+), histamine-producing enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells (Hdc+), somatostatin-producing D cells (Sst+), gastrin-producing G cells (Gast+) and ghrelin-producing X/A cells (Ghrl+) (Fig. 1e, Extended Data Fig. 1b).

### Molecular similarity of functionally related cell types

To assess the transcriptional similarity of epithelial cells between the corpus and antrum, we embedded single-cell expression data from both compartments using UMAP (Fig. 1f, left panel). Overall, the cell types found in both the corpus and antrum (i.e., pit, isthmus, gland base/neck, tuft, EE cells) were closely aligned, as is exemplified by Muc5ac and Muc6 expression patterns (Fig. 1c,d,f right panels). This observation extended globally as MDS analysis revealed that cell types common to both the corpus and antrum generally clustered together, although they were not perfectly aligned (Extended Data Fig. 1c). To determine whether this imperfect alignment of analogous cell types is due to cell type-specific or tissue-wide differences, we searched for transcripts that were differentially expressed in pit, gland base/neck, isthmus, EE or tuft cells between the corpus and antrum. Notably, most differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between pairs of analogous cell types were not specific to any specific cell type but rather were broadly associated with the respective tissue, as is shown for Car9 in the corpus (Fig. 1g, Extended Data Fig. 1d) and Gkn3 in the antrum (Fig. 1g, Extended Data Fig. 1d)(see Extended Data Fig. 1e for summary heatmap).

We next compared our data with single cell expression data from the intestine, which is a similarly organized endoderm-derived epithelium35. Corpus and antrum epithelial cells were overall more similar to one another than to the intestinal epithelial cells using Conos (Extended Data Fig. 1f). However, we detected striking similarities between certain gastric and intestinal cell types. Specifically, tuft cells, as well as EE cells from the stomach and intestine, were transcriptionally highly similar as determined by the joint UMAP embedding as well as common gene expression programs (e.g., Alox5ap, Lrmp, Dckl1 in tuft cells; Chga/b, Insm1, Neurod1 in EE cells) (Extended Data Fig. 1g). Similarly, intestinal Paneth cells, a specialized cell type that secretes antimicrobial defensins, and gastric chief cells, which secrete digestive enzymes, were aligned in our joint UMAP embedding. Consistent with this finding, we detected transcripts for markers previously associated with one of these cell types across both Paneth and chief cells including Clps, Tmed6, Nupr1 and Mist1(Bhlha15)36 (Extended Data Fig. 1g).

### Co-existence of two distinct stem cell populations

We next analyzed the expression of marker genes previously associated with gastric stem cells. Expression of the intestinal marker gene Villin (Vil1) reportedly identifies rare facultative stem cells of unknown identity in the glandular stomach19. Analysis of our single cell data revealed that Vil1 expression is most strongly enriched in cells that also express the tuft cell markers Dclk1 and Alox5ap (Fig. 1c,d, Fig. 2a), consistent with the recent finding that rare Dclk1pos tuft cells harbor stem cell potential18. Another recent study identified gastric stem cells based on Stmn1 expression, which specifically labels proliferative isthmus cells of the corpus9. In agreement with this report, Stmn1 expression largely overlapped with Mki67 expression in the corpus (Extended Data Fig. 2a). However, in the antrum we observed a distinct Stmn1posKi67neg population that overlapped with the EE progenitor cell markers Neurog3 and Sox437,38 (Fig. 2b,c), suggesting that Stmn1 expression may serve as a useful identifier not only for dividing isthmus stem cells in the corpus, but also for EE cell progenitors in the antrum.

Our unbiased mapping of corpus and antrum epithelial cells suggested that the isthmus and gland base are largely distinct cell populations (Fig. 1c,d). However, transcript levels for the gland base-associated marker Lgr513,16 and the isthmus-associated marker Sox28,9,39 were too low in our single cell data to confidently discriminate between these populations (Extended Data Fig. 2b). We therefore attempted to identify additional genes that could differentiate between the gland base and isthmus in the corpus and antrum. Notable genes associated with the gland base included the transcription factors Nfatc4, Prdm2 and Lhx4, the cell polarity gene Insc, and the signaling molecules Wnt5b and Lefty1 in addition to known gland base markers such as Muc6, A4gnt, and Gif (Fig. 2d). We validated the specific expression of Nfatc4, Prdm2 and Insc in the corpus gland base using immunohistochemistry (Fig. 2e). Unexpectedly, we detected other gland base markers such as Sox9, Aqp5, and Spp112,13 in a fraction of isthmus cells (Fig. 2d), suggesting that there may be an underappreciated transitional state between the gland base and isthmus. In support of this notion, a recent study identified multipotent Axin2pos cells in the region connecting the antral gland base and isthmus40.

To corroborate and extend these observations, we purified gland base-enriched (EpcamposLgr5-GFPpos) and isthmus/pit-enriched (EpcamposLgr5-GFPneg) epithelial cells from the antrum and corpus of Lgr5-DTR-GFP mice for bulk RNA-sequencing41. While some gland base markers (e.g., Muc6 and Gif) were exclusively expressed in Lgr5-GFPpos cells of the antrum, other markers (e.g., Aqp5 and Sox9) were also detectable in Lgr5-GFPneg non-gland base cells, consistent with Lgr5 labeling a putative transitional state (Fig. 2f). Notably, Lgr5-GFPpos gland base cells of the corpus could be further subdivided into two populations based on Epcam expression (Fig. 2g). EpcamposLgr5-GFPpos cells expressed the chief cell markers Bhlha15 (Mist1) and Tnfrsf19 (Troy) consistent with a previous report that identified Lgr5 as a chief cell marker in the corpus16. Unexpectedly, EpcamhighLgr5-GFPpos cells expressed the canonical tuft cell markers Dclk1, Trpm5 and Alox5ap, linking gastric Lgr5 expression and tuft cell identity in the corpus (Fig. 2g, Extended Data Fig. 2c).

Closer inspection of the isthmus cluster revealed additional genes that may play a role in the maintenance of isthmus stem cells, including the transcription (co)factors Tcf19, Foxm1, Fbxo5, Birc5 and Hmgb2, the chromatin regulators Ezh2, Set, Asf1b, Setd8, Dnmt1, and Uhrf1 and the histones H2afx, H2afz, and Hist1h2a (Fig. 2d). We validated elevated protein levels for Set, Birc5, and Hmgb2 in cells within the isthmus and early pit using immunohistochemistry (Fig. 2h). Interestingly, isthmus cells also exhibited increased entropy levels42 relative to gland base cells, which suggests that isthmus cells represent a more plastic state compared to gland base/neck cells (Fig. 2i). In agreement with this interpretation, cell cycle analyses showed that the majority of isthmus cells in the antrum and corpus were in the S or G2M phase whereas gland base cells in the antrum and neck cells in the corpus were largely in the G0/G1 phase (Extended Data Fig. 2d).

### Expansion of gastric stem cells as a monolayer

In an effort to permanently capture and study isthmus stem cells in vitro, we tested commercially available media previously developed for the establishment of pseudostratified and stratified epithelial monolayer cultures43. We supplemented this basal media with the Wnt agonists Wnt3a, Rspo1 and CHIR99021 since Wnt signaling was shown to be important for gastric epithelial specification and organoid maintenance13,31 (Fig. 3a, Extended Data Fig. 3a). Additionally, we provided the small molecule A83-01 to inhibit TGFβ signaling because nuclear localization of SMADs coincides with epithelial differentiation43. Finally, we included the growth factor HGF and the Notch agonist Jagged1, two signaling modulators previously associated with gastric stem cell biology44,45. Upon explantation of dissociated murine gastric glands from the corpus or antrum on a layer of irradiated murine embryonic fibroblast feeders using this complete media (referred to as 2D media), we obtained small clusters of epithelial cells that could be expanded and propagated for at least 6 months (>20 passages), demonstrating their ability to continuously self-renew (Fig. 3b).

Selective omission of individual components from our 2D media demonstrated that Wnt activity and TGFβ inhibition were required for epithelial growth, whereas Jagged1 and HGF promoted colony growth but were not essential (Fig 3c, Extended Data Fig. 3b–e). The presence of irradiated feeders was also essential to sustain 2D cultures as feeder-conditioned media or commonly used basement membrane matrices failed to support epithelial growth (Extended Data Fig. 3f–h). In the presence of complete 2D media, epithelial cultures remained karyotypically normal despite repeated passaging (Fig. 3d). We confirmed the glandular gastric identity of these cultures by marker analysis (Fig. 3e) and showed that most cells expressed the isthmus-associated marker Sox2. Additionally, we observed groups of cells expressing the proliferation marker Mki67 adjacent to cells expressing the pit cell marker Muc5ac within each colony, suggesting that 2D media selects for immature cells that spontaneously differentiate into mucin-producing pit-like cells (Fig. 3f).

To determine the cellular composition of antral and corpus 2D cultures relative to the primary stomach, we performed single cell RNA-sequencing. Cultured 2D corpus and antrum samples formed a continuum of transcriptionally related cells that aligned closest to primary isthmus progenitors transitioning towards the differentiated pit cell lineage (Fig. 3g). Consistent with this trajectory, isthmus-like 2D cells had a higher average entropy score than the pit-like cells (Extended Data Fig. 4a) and expressed several isthmus (Hmgb2 and Birc5) and pit (Tff1 and Klf4) markers (Fig. 3h, Extended Data Fig. 4b). We also detected a rare subset of cells within 2D cultures that closely aligned with primary gland base/neck cells and expressed the gland base/neck markers Gkn3, Aqp5 and Muc6 (Fig. 3h, Extended Data Fig. 4b). Lastly, we identified infrequent 2D cells that closely aligned with corpus chief cells (Fig. 3g). Thus, 2D cultures in self-renewal conditions are predominantly composed of isthmus-like and pit-like cells with a small number of gland base-like as well as chief-like cells.

### 2D cultures maintain a memory of their tissue of origin

To explore whether 2D cultures maintain a memory of their tissue of origin, we compared bulk RNA-sequencing data from corpus- and antrum-derived 2D cells. Most genes were similarly expressed between 2D corpus and antrum cultures as expected (Fig. 3i, left panel). However, we did identify 308 DEGs, some of which also discriminated between primary corpus and antrum including the antral EE cell marker Nkx6-3 and the corpus parietal cell marker Esrrg (Fig. 3i, right panel, Extended Data Fig. 4c,d). Accordingly, we detected protein expression of the murine chief cell marker Gif exclusively in corpus 2D cultures, confirming the identity of chief-like cells in the single cell analysis (Fig. 3i,j, Extended Data Fig. 4e). Additionally, the corpus 2D expression signature most closely aligned with the primary corpus expression signature, while the antrum 2D expression signature most closely resembled the primary antrum expression signature, supporting the notion that 2D cultures indeed retain a transcriptional memory of their tissue of origin (Fig. 3k).

To investigate whether the observed transcriptional memory of corpus vs. antrum 2D cultures restricts their differentiation potential into EE cell types, we adopted a differentiation protocol previously established for intestinal-derived organoids46 (Fig. 3l, top panel). As expected, Sst and Ghrl were upregulated to a similar degree in antral and corpus EE cell cultures, consistent with the presence of both D and X/A cells throughout the glandular stomach (Fig. 3l, center panel). By contrast, Gast and Tph1 expression were higher in antrum-derived cultures, consistent with the enrichment of G and EC cells in the primary antrum. Likewise, Hdc expression was higher in corpus-derived 2D cultures, mirroring the enrichment of ECL cells in the primary corpus. We confirmed the induction of EE cell markers at the protein level as rare, morphologically distinct 5-HTpos cells were found throughout the differentiated antrum 2D culture, corresponding to the increased RNA expression of the EC cell marker Tph1 in culture (Fig. 3l, middle and bottom panels).

### Derivation of gastric 2D cultures from human stomach

When we dissociated and explanted human stomach mucosa in 2D media (Extended Data Fig. 5a), colonies emerged and gave rise to stable 2D cultures that could be propagated for at least 6 months, demonstrating the ability to indefinitely self-renew (Extended Data Fig. 5b). Similar to mouse 2D cultures, the majority of human 2D cultures expressed SOX2 (Fig. 4a), while the proliferation marker KI67 and pit cell markers MUC5AC and GKN1 were scattered throughout the colonies (Fig. 4a, Extended Data Fig. 5c). Human 2D cultures also secreted MUC5AC into the media, confirming their spontaneous differentiation into functional pit-like cells (Fig. 4b). Single cell RNA-sequencing of antrum- and corpus-derived cell lines (n=2 individuals) yielded four discernible clusters, with clusters 1 to 3 being closely related and cluster 4 being more distinct (Fig. 4c). Differential gene expression analysis suggested that clusters 1-3 are comprised of proliferative isthmus-like cells that spontaneously differentiate into immature and mature pit-like cells (Extended Data Fig. 5d). For instance, the isthmus-associated markers MKI67, TOP2A and CCNB1 were upregulated in cluster 1, whereas the pit cell-associated markers KRT18 and TFF2 were upregulated in clusters 2 and 3, respectively (Fig. 4d, Extended Data Fig. 5d). This differentiation trajectory from immature to mature pit cells is also reflected by the sequential upregulation of the mucins MUC1 and MUC5AC in clusters 2 and 3 (Fig. 4e, left panel). Supporting the physiological relevance of this transition, we found MUC1-expressing putative transitional cells enriched in the center of gastric units above the gland base, while MUC5AC-expressing pit cells are enriched on the luminal surface (Fig. 4e, right panels). Unexpectedly, we did not detect gland base/neck markers such as LGR5, AQP5, INSC, NFATC4 and SLC9A4 in human 2D cultures, suggesting that gland base/neck cells are either extremely rare in human 2D cultures or cannot be maintained (Extended Data Fig. 5e). Moreover, we detected a group of cells (cluster 4) that appears to be specific to human 2D cultures and is defined by the expression of inflammatory mediators such as CXCL8 (IL2) (Fig. 4f).

To assess whether human 2D cultures can give rise to additional gastric cell types not detected in self-renewal conditions, we cultured 2D cells using air-liquid interface (ALI) inserts (Extended Data Fig. 6a). We detected abundant cells with apical expression of the pit cell marker MUC5AC in both antrum and corpus ALI cultures (Fig 4g). Additionally, we detected rare cells exclusively in the corpus ALI cultures that exhibited apical expression of gastric intrinsic factor (GIF), a protein expressed in human parietal cells47 (Fig. 4h, Extended Data Fig. 6b). We also detected the expression of hormones associated with several EE-like cell types, including EC-like cells (5-HT+), D-like Cells (SST+) and G-like cells (GAST+) (Fig. 4h). Notably, these hormones were trafficked to the basal side of cells in ALI cultures, consistent with their secretion into the submucosal space in vivo.

To define similarities and differences between mouse and human gastric epithelia, we compared our 2D single cell data from each species. Mouse and human cells aligned as a homogeneous population, although we observed some species-specific subclustering (Fig. 4i). Gene expression of mouse and human samples were highly correlated (R=0.8), supporting and extending a previous report that compared human and mouse primary stomach21 (Extended Data Fig. 6c). However, we also detected genes that were selectively upregulated in mouse or human cells and likely reflect compositional differences between 2D cultures. For example, the pit cell markers TFF1, TFF2, MUC5AC, and the chief/neck cell marker PGC were upregulated in human 2D-cultured cells (Fig. 4j). Genes more broadly expressed in primary mouse gastric epithelia such as Clu were also upregulated in mouse 2D cultures compared to human 2D cultures (Fig. 4j, Extended Data Fig. 6d). Of interest, despite the species-specific separation of most cells in the Conos embedding (Fig. 4I), unbiased clustering grouped gastric cells based on their function rather than their origin from mouse or human, suggesting that cell statespecific transcriptional differences are dominant over species-specific transcriptional differences (Fig. 4k, Extended Data Fig. 6e–g).

### Wnt-responsive Lgr5neg cells facilitate 2D culture expansion

To define molecular and cellular differences between conventional 3D and our 2D gastric culture system, we derived isogenic 3D organoids and 2D cultures using stomachs from Lgr5DTR-GFP reporter mice41. 2D cultures contained ~5% Lgr5-GFPpos cells, similar to the percentage of Lgr5pos cells found in vivo48, while organoids contained ~19% Lgr5pos cells, suggesting that organoid conditions enrich for gland base cells (Fig. 5a, Extended Data Fig. 7a). Global gene expression analysis revealed that 2D corpus and 2D antrum cultures were transcriptionally more similar to each other (308 DEGs, see Fig. 3g) than to organoids (over 3,000 DEGs)(Fig. 5b,c). Importantly, DEGs upregulated in 2D cultures relative to organoids included markers associated with the isthmus (e.g., Stmn1, Hmgb2, Set) and pit (e.g., Muc5ac, Klf4, Gkn1/2) (Fig. 5d). Conversely, DEGs upregulated in organoids relative to 2D cultures included the gland base/neck-associated markers Muc6, Gkn3, Lgr5 and Sox9 (Fig. 5d). We corroborated this conclusion by single cell expression analysis of our 2D and organoid cultures (Fig. 5e), which showed that isthmus- and pit-associated markers (Hmgb2/Birc5, Klf4/Tff1) were overrepresented in 2D culture, whereas gland base/neck-associated markers (Muc6, Aqp5) were overrepresented in organoid culture (Fig. 5f, Extended Data Fig. 7b). Moreover, 2D cultures appeared to be more transcriptionally heterogeneous than organoid cultures, suggesting that 2D cultures are more plastic than organoid cultures (Fig. 5g,h).

Previous reports suggested that Lgr5pos gland base cells are required for the long-term maintenance of gastric organoid cultures10,12,13. To test whether Lgr5-GFPpos cells are similarly required for the maintenance of 2D cultures, we exposed Lgr5DTR-GFP 2D cultures to diphtheria toxin (DT), allowing us to ablate Lgr5-GFPpos cells in vitro (Fig. 5i). Remarkably, DT treatment had no measurable short-term or long-term effect on the proliferation rate of 2D cultures despite the loss of Lgr5-GFPpos cells, consistent with the ability of human 2D cultures to expand without a discernable gland base population (Extended Data Fig. 7c). Moreover, withdrawal of DT from mouse 2D cultures led to the gradual re-emergence of Lgr5-GFPpos cells (Fig. 5j). By contrast, treatment of Lgr5DTR-GFP organoids with DT led to a progressive decrease in the number of organoids, as expected (Extended Data Fig. 7d). Of note, we observed a significant reduction in the size of gastric Lgr5GFP-DTR colonies upon Wnt inhibition and concomitant DT treatment, suggesting that Lgr5− isthmus-like cells require Wnt signaling to maintain an undifferentiated, proliferative state (Fig. 5k).

### Interconversion of 2D cultures and organoid cultures

Considering that murine 2D cultures contain a rare population of gland base-like Lgr5pos cells (Fig. 5a) and organoids contain a rare population of isthmus-like Hmgb2pos cells (Fig. 5f), we hypothesized that 2D cells can be converted to organoids and vice versa (Fig. 6a, top panel). Indeed, dissociated 2D cells from the antrum and corpus readily gave rise to 3D organoids that could be repeatedly passaged, while dissociated corpus and antrum organoids readily transitioned to 2D culture conditions and could be maintained long-term (Fig. 6a, bottom panel). Corpus and antrum organoids derived from 2D cultures were morphologically and molecularly indistinguishable from conventional organoids as exemplified by the upregulation of gland base/neck markers (e.g., Lgr5, Muc6, Tff2) and the downregulation of isthmus/pit markers (e.g., Tff1, Muc5ac) (Fig. 6b, light colored bars, Extended Data Fig. 8a). Conversely, the re-plating of corpus or antrum organoids in 2D culture conditions facilitated a reciprocal molecular switch towards 2D culture identity (Extended Data Fig. 8b,c). Strikingly, Lgr5-GFPpos cells FACS-purified from 2D cultures had a ~10-fold higher potential to initiate organoid growth compared to Lgr5-GFPneg cells, suggesting that the Lgr5pos cells in 2D culture are functional gland base-like cells (Fig. 6c,d). Surprisingly, rare organoids emerged from sorted Lgr5-GFPneg cells and gradually restored Lgr5-GFP expression (Fig. 6e), raising the possibility that rare Lgr5-GFPpos cells contaminated the flow-sorted Lgr5-GFPneg population (Extended Data Fig. 8d,e). In support of this notion, we were unable to derive stable organoids from Lgr5-DTR-GFP 2D culture when DT was added during the conversion (Fig. 6f).

### Sox2 levels distinguish isthmus from enterochromaffin cells

Based on our finding that Lgr5pos cells are dispensable for 2D culture maintenance, we hypothesized that isthmus cells selectively give rise to 2D cultures. To enrich for isthmus cells, we generated a Sox2-E2A-tdTomato knock-in reporter mouse strain. We detected Sox2neg, Sox2pos, and rare Sox2high cells in the antrum of our transgenic mice by flow cytometry, confirming our prior observations39 (Fig. 7a, left panel). There was good overlap between endogenous Sox2 protein and Sox2 reporter signal in the isthmus region of the antrum (Extended Data Fig. 9a) as well as in the isthmus and gland base region of the corpus (Fig. 7a, right panel, Extended Data Fig. 9b). Consistent with this enrichment pattern in the corpus, RNA-sequencing of sorted Tomato subpopulations showed upregulation of the gland base/chief cell markers Lgr5, Pgc, Gif and Troy in Sox2pos cells compared to Sox2neg cells (Extended Data Fig. 9c).

We next sorted five cells each of Lgr5-GFPneg, Lgr5-GFPpos, Sox2neg, Sox2pos, and Sox2high gastric epithelial cells isolated from the antrum into single wells of 96-well plates and counted colonies after 10 days of expansion using 2D media. While the colony-forming potential of Sox2neg cells was extremely low (~4%) as expected, a sizable fraction of wells plated with Sox2pos cells (~35%) contained colonies (Fig. 7b). Unexpectedly, the colony-forming potential of Sox2high cells were less efficient than Sox2neg cells (~3%). Moreover, Lgr5-GFPpos and Lgr5-GFPneg cells had comparable colony-initiation potential (~13%) which was significantly lower than that of Sox2pos cells. Thus, Sox2pos putative isthmus cells are the predominant cells of origin for antral 2D cultures while the expression levels of Lgr5 do not predict colony-initiation potential (Fig. 7b).

RNA-Sequencing of sorted Sox2neg, Sox2pos and Sox2high cells from the antrum of reporter mice confirmed the overall correlation between endogenous Sox2 mRNA and reporter gene expression (Extended Data Fig. 9d). Additionally, we observed higher expression levels of isthmus markers in Sox2pos cells than in Sox2high cells, suggesting that Sox2pos cells enrich for isthmus cells whereas Sox2high cells are a different cell type (Extended Data Fig. 9e). Indeed, gene ontology (GO) analysis revealed that Sox2high cells are enriched for categories associated with neuronal function and synapse organization pointing to a possible link between high Sox2 expression and EE cell fate (Fig. 7c). Moreover, gastric cells with the highest Sox2 levels co-expressed Tph1, the rate-limiting enzyme for serotonin (5-HT) production and a marker for EC cells (Fig. 7d). Consistent with an EC cell identity of Sox2high cells, antral cells with the highest level of Sox2 protein were also 5-HTpos and were more dendritic by morphology (Fig. 7e). Several other EE and EC cell marker genes were upregulated in Sox2high cells compared to Sox2pos cells, including Nov and Lmx1a as well as Chga and Chgb (Fig. 7f, Extended Data Fig. 9f). Finally, when we compared our RNA-sequencing data of Sox2pos (putative isthmus) and Sox2high (putative EC) cells with a recent dataset of epithelial (ChgA-GFP−) and EC cells (ChgA-GFPpos) isolated from the intestine49, we observed a positive correlation between EC cells across these tissues (Extended Data Fig. 9g). The correlation between SOX2 expression and EC cell fate extended to human stomach, as we detected double-positive 5-HTpos/SOX2high cells in human antrum sections (Extended Data Fig. 9h).

### Sox2 is necessary and sufficient for gastric EC cell specification

Acute loss of Sox2 in the adult stomach does not compromise tissue maintenance, although subtle changes in gene expression were observed39. We therefore compared transcripts previously shown to be downregulated in Sox2 knockout stomachs with transcripts enriched in Sox2high cells (Fig. 7g). Strikingly, over one-third of genes downregulated in Sox2 knockout stomachs (13/33) were overexpressed in Sox2high cells including Tph1, Chgb, Nkx6.1, and Ascl1, suggesting that Sox2 may be crucial for EC cell specification (Fig. 7h).

To test whether Sox2 is required for EC cell specification, we induced EE cell differentiation of 2D antral cultures carrying a conditional Sox2 allele (Sox2fl/fl) as well as a Rosa26-CreER allele (Fig. 7i). Indeed, differentiated 2D cultures lacking Sox2 were unable to upregulate the EC cell marker Tph1 compared to controls, while transcripts associated with other EE cell subtypes including G cells, D cells and ECL cells were not affected. Moreover, when we analyzed antral sections of Sox2fl/fl; Rosa26-CreER mice that had been treated with a pulse of tamoxifen 6 months earlier, we detected a striking loss of 5-HTpos cells, indicating that Sox2 is essential for EC formation or maintenance in vivo (Fig. 7j, Extended Data Fig 9i). Conversely, forced expression of an exogenous Sox2 transgene50 for 2 weeks led to a significant increase of 5-HTpos cells, indicating that Sox2 is sufficient for EC cell specification in vivo (Fig. 7j, Extended Data Fig 9i).

## Discussion

While the antrum and corpus of the glandular stomach represent different tissues with highly specialized functions, we found that cell types with analogous physiological roles across these compartments are remarkably similar at the transcriptional level. Two cell populations of particular interest to us were the poorly characterized isthmus cells and the better characterized gland base cells as they had previously been shown to function as stem cells in the corpus and antrum. We identified several chromatin and transcription factors that are enriched in the gland base (e.g., Nfatc4, Prdm2) and isthmus (e.g., Hmgb2, Set) regions across the glandular stomach. Moreover, we observed that certain gland base markers such as Aqp5 and Spp1 are expressed in a subset of isthmus cells in the antrum, pointing to a dynamic equilibrium between these stem cell zones. These data offer a crucial molecular and cellular framework for the future functional dissection of gland base and isthmus cell populations in vitro and in vivo.

Our single cell data of isthmus and gland base cells facilitated the establishment of a culture system that permanently captures isthmus-like stem cells from the corpus and antrum in mice and humans. This 2D culture system allowed for the long-term self-renewal of epithelial stem cells while maintaining the ability to produce cells that transcriptionally resemble gland base, pit, parietal, chief, and EE cells in culture, thus recapitulating key processes of epithelial regeneration and differentiation in vitro. The predisposition of 2D cultures to generate cell types specific to their tissue of origin could be exploited in the future to generate homogeneous populations of corpus-specific and antrum-specific cell types upon modulation of relevant signaling or genetic pathways. Our results further demonstrate that gastric organoids and 2D cultures can be interconverted by simply switching environmental cues and this process is associated with a commensurate transcriptional rewiring of cell states. These observations underscore the remarkable plasticity that exists between isthmus and gland base cells40,51

Finally, our 2D system helped us determine that high Sox2 levels mark terminally differentiated EC cells whereas low Sox2 levels correlate with isthmus stem cells. Critically, we demonstrate that Sox2 is necessary and sufficient to drive EC specification. Our finding that Sox2 expression levels differentiate between isthmus and EC cells mirrors recent observations in the intestine where low Sox9 levels mark proliferative stem and progenitor cells while high Sox9 levels mark EE progenitors and tuft cells52,53. These results support the notion that Sox factors have context-specific roles that depend on their expression levels and the presence of cofactors54.

In summary, we have developed a tractable and scalable gastric monolayer culture system that has allowed us to gain fundamental insights into the role of specific stem and differentiated cells during gastric epithelial regeneration. We anticipate our model will provide a powerful complementary system to conventional organoids for the genetic, cellular, and biochemical dissection of stomach development, homeostasis, and cancer.

## Methods

### Mice

For all single cell RNA sequencing experiments, 6–8-week-old female or male C57BL/6 wildtype mice were used and obtained from the Jackson Laboratory. The Lgr5-DTR-GFP mouse strain was obtained with permission from Frederic de Sauvage (Genetech)41 and the Rosa26-LSL-Sox2 mouse strain was obtained with permission from Mark Onaitis50. The Sox2 cKO mice was previously published by the Hochedlinger lab39. Mice used in this study were housed and bred in Specific Pathogen Free (SPF) rooms located in the AAALAC-accredited Center for Comparative Medicine vivarium at Massachusetts General Hospital. Mice were housed in ventilated cages on a standard 12:12 light cycle. All procedures involving mice adhered to the guidelines of the approved Massachusetts General Hospital Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) protocol no. 2006N000104.

### Generation of the Sox2 reporter

Sox2tdTomato reporter ESC lines were generated through CRISPR/Cas-mediated gene targeting. A targeting construct was designed to integrate an E2A-tdTomato cassette in-frame with the final exon of Sox2 and generated via PCR amplification such that the E2A-tdTomato cassette was flanked on either side by 500bp of homology to the 3’ end of the Sox2 locus. The targeting construct was cotransfected using Lipofectamine 2000 (Thermo) with a Sox2-targeting sgRNA (5’-AGCCCTCACATGTGCGACAG-3’) and a Cas9 expression construct into V6.5 ESCs. One week following the transfection, tdTomatopos cells were isolated by FACS and clonally expanded for analysis by Southern blot. Positive clones were injected into blastocysts and germline chimeras were bred to establish a Sox2tdTomato-expressing mouse line.

### Gastric gland isolation and cell dissociation

The corpus or antrum of C57BL/6J wild type mice was isolated and repeatedly washed in cold PBS. The surface mucosal layer was gently scraped away from the underlying epithelium using angled forceps (FST 00276-13) and the epithelium was vortexed in ice-cold PBS. The tissues were incubated in 6 mL of Cell Recovery Solution (Corning) for 30 minutes on ice, with gentle shaking every five minutes. For antral gland dissociation, the tissue was placed in 1mL of cell recovery solution in a 6 cm dish, and the glands were gently scraped off of the underlying mesenchyme using angled forceps under a stereomicroscope. A p1000 tip was then used to slowly pipette the glands until individual glands could be uniformly seen. The glands remained in cell recovery solution and were placed in an Eppendorf tube on ice while the remaining tissues were dissociated. For corpus gland dissociation, the tissue was placed in 1mL of cell recovery solution in a 6 cm dish and the glands were gently pinched off the underlying mesenchyme and muscle using angled forceps under a stereomicroscope. A p1000 tip was then used to slowly pipette the glands until single glands could be uniformly seen. The glands remained in cell recovery solution and were placed in an Eppendorf tube on ice until all tissues were dissociated. Antral or corpus glands corresponding to one stomach were spun down at 300g for 3 minutes and cells were dissociated with 1mL 0.25% trypsin +EDTA (Gibco) for exactly 5 minutes at 20°C while being briefly vortexed every minute. The trypsin was quenched using 500uL of ice-cold PBS containing 2% FBS and the cells were passed through a 40-um filter and spun down at 300g for 5 minutes. The single cell suspension was then stained for FACS for scRNA-seq (below) direct analysis.

### Gastric organoid culture

Following gland isolation (see above), the antrum or corpus glands obtained from each stomach were spun down and embedded in 50 uL x 3 GFR Matrigel with phenol red (Corning) into 3 wells of a 24 well plate and incubated at 37°C until the Matrigel solidified. Matrigel with the embedded corpus or antral glands were incubated in 1mL of culture media which was made using the following protocol: 50% advanced DMEM/F12 (Invitrogen) supplemented with 20% FBS (Hyclone), N2 (1X, Life Technologies), B27 (1X, Life Technologies), 1X plasmocin and 1X primocin (Invivogen), and 50% conditioned media containing Wnt3A, R-spondin-1, and Noggin (WRN, ATCC). The combined media was supplemented with 50 ng/mL EGF (Peprotech), 100ng/mL FGF10 (Peprotech), 10uM Gastrin (Sigma), 1uM CHIR99021 (Tocris), and 10uM Y-27632 (Tocris). Fresh media was replaced every other day, and organoids were passaged every 6 days 1:3 by dissolving Matrigel using cell recovery solution (Corning) and mechanically breaking up organoids by pipetting up and down 30-50 times using a p200 pipette. For experiments requiring diphtheria toxin treatment, 10ng/mL of diphtheria toxin (Sigma) was added to the culture every other day for the duration of the experiment.

### 2D gastric epithelial culture

Following gland isolation for mouse tissue (see above), antral or corpus glands obtained from each stomach were spun down and allowed to settle on confluent, irradiated CD-1 mouse embryonic fibroblasts (derived in house) preplated on a T25 flask. Both the irradiated feeders and the explanted gastric cells were incubated with 2D media which was made using the following protocol: 70% SABM media (Lonza) containing all the included supplements, 1X plasmocin and 1X primocin antibiotics (invivogen), 1μM CHIR99021 (Tocris), 1μM A83-01 (Tocris), 10μM Y-27632 (Tocris), and 30% of 1:1 mixture of conditioned media containing Wnt3A (using cell line L Wnt3A, ATCC) and conditioned media containing R-spondin-1 (using cell line 3710-001, Trevigen). Wnt3a and Rspo1 conditioned media was generated using advanced DMEM/F12 (Gibco), 10% FBS (hyclone), and 1X plasmocin and primocin antibiotics (invivogen). Complete 2D media was then supplemented with 1μM Jagged-1 (Anaspec) and 50 ng/mL HGF (Peprotech). Fresh media was replaced every other day and split 1:5 once cells reached ~75% confluency. Cells were frozen down using CryoStor CS10 (Stemcell Technologies). For air liquid-interface culture of human 2D cells, a confluent T25 flask was split into a single 6-well 0.4um transwell insert (Stemcell Technologies) and 2D culture media was applied both above and below the culture. The next day the cells that did not attach were removed and 2D media was overlayed on the culture for an additional 48 hours to ensure the formation of tight junctions and loss of feeders. Media was then removed from the top of the transwell and 2D media was replaced every 4 days. Every week, PBS was gently applied to the top of the culture to remove accumulating mucus. For experiments requiring diphtheria toxin treatment, 10ng/mL of diphtheria toxin (Sigma) was added to the culture every other day for the duration of the experiment. For single cell sequencing and RNA extraction, trypsin preferentially detached the feeder layer from the culture. When all the feeders detached, the trypsin and dissociated feeders were removed, fresh trypsin was reapplied, and the culture was incubated at 37°C until the epithelial cells detached and could be harvested. For experiments using recombinant Wnt/Rspo as opposed to Wnt/Rspo conditioned media, a final concentration of 100ng/mL of Wnt3a (315-20, Peprotech) and 1ug/mL Rspo1 (315-32, Peprotech) was used.

### In vitro enteroendocrine differentiation

2D-cultured cells were grown to confluency and cultured in differentiation media consisting of 70% SABM containing all the included growth factors, 1X plasmocin and primocin antibiotics (invivogen), and 30% conditioned media containing Wnt3a, Rspondin-1, and Noggin (L-WRN, ATCC). The complete media was supplemented with 1.5μM IWP2 (Tocris), 10μM DAPT (Tocris), and 1μM PD0325901 (Tocris). Epithelial cells were cultured in differentiation conditions for a period of 72 hours before harvesting for RNA or fixed for immunofluorescence.

## Keratinocyte & forestomach culture

Adult forestomach was removed from wildtype mice, sliced into 1-3 mm pieces, cleaned in ice cold PBS, and rocked for no more than 10 hours at 4°C in dissociation media comprised of DMEM/F12 (Gibco), 200 μg/mL Pronase (Sigma), 10 μg/mL Dnase I (Worthington), 1% Fraction V BSA (Gibco), 1X pen/strep, and 10 μM Y-27632 (Tocris). Tissue was spun down at 300g for 5 minutes and cells/tissue was brought up in cold PBS, pipetted up and down 20 times using a p1000 pipette and filtered through a 100μm filter. Human neonatal keratinocytes (Invitrogen) or dissociated mouse forestomach was explanted onto T25 flasks precoated with conditioned media harvested from 804G cells43. Complete SAGM media supplemented with 10μM Y-27632 (Tocris), 1μM CHIR99021 (Tocris), 1μM A83-01, and 1μM DMH-1 (only used for forestomach culture, Tocris) was used for expansion. Cells were fed every day and split 1:8 when 75% confluency was reached.

### Human gastric gland isolation

Human gastric tissue was obtained from male and female patients that underwent a sleeve gastrectomy procedure in accordance with Massachusetts General Hospital IRB 2018P002715, and their informed consent. Approximately 2 cm2 piece of mucosa and underlying mesenchyme was placed on ice-cold PBS and vortexed vigorously for several minutes to loosen the intercalating and surface mucus from the epithelium. The epithelium was combed with angled forceps and briefly vortexed to remove accumulating mucus multiple times for a period of 30-45 minutes. Once mucus ceased to form on the surface of the tissue it was cut into smaller 5mm2 pieces and placed in a 50 mL conical tube containing 20mL of ice-cold cell recovery solution (Corning) supplemented with 10μM Y-27632 for 1 hour and shaken every 10 minutes. Glands were then gently combed to remove any residual mucus, washed in fresh cell recovery solution, and separated from the underlying mesenchyme by pinching off individual glands using angled forceps under a stereomicroscope. Individual glands were then washed several times in cold PBS and plated down using the same protocol used for explanting mouse gastric glands.

### Immunofluorescence/Immunohistochemistry

Paraffin and frozen embedding were performed using standard protocols. Antigen retrieval was performed on paraffin-embedded sections using a sodium citrate solution (Vector Labs). Antibodies used for this study are as follows: Ki67 (Invitrogen 14-5698-82 1:500 dilution), Muc5AC (Invitrogen MA5-12178 1:50 dilution), Epcam (Biolegend 324202 conjugated to Alexa 594 1:500 dilution), Epcam (Biolegend 118202 conjugated to Alexa 594 1:500 dilution), 5-HT (Immunostar 20080 1:1000 dilution), Sst (Immunostar 20067 1:1000 dilution), Gast (Immunostar n/a 1:1000 dilution), Gif (gift from Dr. Alpers 1:400 dilution), Sox2 (R&D AF2018 1:100 dilution), Zo-1 (Thermo 33-9100 1:100 dilution), Muc1 (Invitrogen MA5-11202 1:200 dilution), Birc5 (Cell Signaling 71G4B7 1:100 dilution), Insc (Sigma HPA039769 1:100 dilution), Hmgb2 (Proteintech 14597-1-AP 1:100 dilution), Nfatc4 (Invitrogen PA1-021 1:500 dilution), Prdm2 (Sigma HPA005809 1:100 dilution), Set (Bethyl Labs A302-261A 1:500 dilution), Gkn1 (R&D AF7287 1:50 dilution), tdTomato (Rockland 200-301-379 1:500 dilution), GFP (Rockland 600-901-215 1:500 dilution), RFP (Rockland 600-401-379 1:500 dilution).

## Cell sorting

Mouse primary sorted cells were isolated using the previously described protocol, passed through a 40uM filter, and stained for Epcam (clone 9C4, Biolegend), AnnexinV (Biogend), and DAPI using the AnnexinV staining protocol and buffers. Epcampos/AnnexinVneg/DAPIneg cells were then sorted and GFP or TdTomato was analyzed when applicable. For mouse and human 2D cells, cells were stained with Epcam and DAPI to exclude irradiated feeders and dead cells. For organoid sorting, DAPI was used to exclude dead cells.

### Single-cell encapsulation, library prep, and sequencing

#### Primary mouse epithelia.

Primary cells were sorted as described above and encapsulated using the inDrops method as previously described34 Briefly, a microfluidic device was used to co-encapsulate individual cells and hydrogel beads carrying barcoding reverse transcription (RT) primers into 2–3 nl droplets. After a RT reaction, droplets were broken, and the resulting bulk material was taken through second strand synthesis, in vitro transcription providing linear amplification of the material, fragmentation of the amplified RNA, a second reverse transcription, and finally PCR, yielding in a sequencing-ready library.

#### Cultured cells.

Corpus and antrum 2D-cultured cells were passaged 3 times, sorted as described above, and encapsulated using the chromium 10x platform V2 according to the manufacturer’s protocol using 5,000 cells per lane. Libraries for these cells were also performed as described in the 10X protocol.

### Computational analysis of single-cell data

The sequenced libraries were demultiplexed using dropEst55 and aligned to mm10 assembly. Cells with at least 1000 molecules were used for subsequent analysis. The datasets were integrated using Conos56, using PCA space, default parameters, using 2000 top overdispersed genes and 30 top eigenvectors per dataset pair. The samples were then visualized using UMAP embedding, and initial subpopulations of cells were determined using Leiden algorithm (r=1). Annotation was carried out manually with the help of pagoda2 browser (https://github.com/kharchenkolab/pagoda2/), based on the differentially expressed genes and known literature markers. Entropy estimates were obtained using entropy R package. Multidimensional scaling was calculated using cmdscale() function in R on the aggregate profiles of each subpopulation: combining molecules across all cells, using log10[c*S/N +1] expression values, where c is the total count of molecules observed for a given gene in a given cell population, N is the total number of molecules observed in that subpopulation across all genes, and S=1000 is the library size constant. Conos integration was carried out using pagoda2 pre-processing (using basicP2proc() function from pagoda2 package). Cell cycle status of profiled cells was performed using a raw counts matrix for combined primary stomach data to create a Seurat57 object with min.cells=3 and min.features=200 options. Data was normalized and scaled prior to CellCycleScoring(). Cell cycle S and G2M genes for human were downloaded from https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hbc/tinyatlas/master/cell_cycle/Homo_sapiens.csv and mouse orthologs defined by using biomaRt. For comparison between mouse and human 2D cultures, 1-to-1 orthologous genes for two species were obtained by using biomaRt58 package for R and limiting the count matrices of each sample to these genes.

Vim-positive cells (read counts > 2) and cells with abundant mitochondrial genes expression (Mt > 20%) were filtered out. Next, the matrices of technical replicates were merged and processed with default parameters using mergeCountMatrices(), and Conos integration was carried out using pagoda2 pre-processing (using basicP2proc() function from pagoda2 package). Cross-species graph and cell clusters were obtained by using Conos buildGraph() and findCommunities(method=leiden.community, resolution=0.4) functions. Differential expression analysis between human and mouse was performed on pseudo bulk by using the edgeR59 package for R. Data was TMM normalized, common and tagwise dispersion calculated, and differentially expressed genes defined with glmFit and glmLRT functions (FDR < 0.05). Correlation analysis for human and mouse orthologous genes was performed on pseudo bulk counts using two-sided Pearson correlation test. Transcriptional heterogeneity between cells was calculated by using expression distances obtained using the Cacoa version 0.2.0 estimateExpressionShiftMagnitudes() function, which estimates distances between samples using correlation distance on gene expression vectors. Normalized expression shift vectors and the overall expression distances between samples were determined as a normalized weighted sum of correlation distances across all cell subpopulations contained in both samples.

### Gene expression quantification by quantitative PCR

Cultured stratified and/or glandular epithelial cells were dissociated as previously described, and RNA was isolated using trizol and the RNeasy kit (Qiagen) according to the manufacturer's protocol. cDNA was generated using the High Capacity cDNA reverse transcriptase kit (Applied Biosystems). Realtime quantitative PCR was performed using validated primers and the Brilliant III Sybr green master mix (Agilent) on a Roche lightcycler 480 system. All experiments were normalized to Gapdh. Relative quantification was performed using the ΔΔCt method. Primer sequences used are listed in Supplementary table 1.

### ELISA

Human 2D cultures corresponding to three individuals were expanded and once 50-60% confluency was reached, 2D media was harvested from each sample after being exposed to the 2D cells for a period of 24 hours. Media was then tested for secreted mucins in the supernatant using double-antibody sandwich ELISA kit for Muc5AC (TSZ Scientific). Human neonatal keratinocytes cultured as previously described were used as a control.

### Statistics and Reproducibility

Statistical tests are described in the corresponding figure legends. Unless otherwise indicated, statistical analyses were carried out using GraphPad Prism. Data distribution was assumed to be normal but this was not formally tested. For Figs. 2e, 2h, 3b, 3f, 3j, 3l, 4a, 4e, 4g–h, 7e, 7j, and Extended Data Figs. 3a–b, 3e–h, 4e, 5b–c, 6b, 9a–b,9h, data are representative images of three independent experiments. No statistical method was used to predetermine sample size, no data were excluded from the analyses, and the investigators were not blinded to allocation during experiments and outcome assessment.

Introduction The cohesin complex is a multimeric protein complex that forms a ring structure around DNA molecules and plays multiple key roles in spatial organization of eukaryotic genomes. Cohesin proteins are involved in several essential cellular functions, including sister chromatid cohesion, chromatin loop organization, transcriptional activation, and DNA replication and damage repair, among others (reviewed in ref. 1). More recently, the cohesin complex was identified as one of the most frequently mutated protein complexes in cancer, including myeloid malignancies, glioblastoma, breast cancer, bladder cancer, and Ewing sarcoma (2, 3). The mechanisms by which cohesin mutations cause cellular transformation are unknown, and currently no therapies are known to exhibit selective efficacy in cohesin-mutant cancers. Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) and acute myeloid leukemia (AML) are clonal diseases of mutated hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) characterized by abnormal differentiation and proliferation caused by somatic mutations in genes encoding transcription factors, epigenetic regulators, chromatin modifiers, and splicing factors (4, 5). The core components of the cohesin complex, stromal antigen 2 (STAG2), structural maintenance of chromosomes 1 (SMC1), SMC3, and RAD21, as well as its modulators, PDS5 and NIPBL cohesin loading factor (NIPBL), are collectively mutated in 13% of patients with de novo AML, 21% of patients with secondary AML, and 11% of patients with MDS, where they are associated with poor overall survival (5–10). The cohesin complex plays an essential role in chromosome maintenance and transcriptional regulation. Recurrent somatic mutations in the cohesin complex are frequent genetic drivers in cancer, including myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) and acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Here, using genetic dependency screens of stromal antigen 2–mutant (STAG2-mutant) AML, we identified DNA damage repair and replication as genetic dependencies in cohesin-mutant cells. We demonstrated increased levels of DNA damage and sensitivity of cohesin-mutant cells to poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibition. We developed a mouse model of MDS in which Stag2 mutations arose as clonal secondary lesions in the background of clonal hematopoiesis driven by tet methylcytosine dioxygenase 2 (Tet2) mutations and demonstrated selective depletion of cohesinmutant cells with PARP inhibition in vivo. Finally, we demonstrated a shift from STAG2- to STAG1- containing cohesin complexes in cohesin-mutant cells, which was associated with longer DNA loop extrusion, more intermixing of chromatin compartments, and increased interaction with PARP and replication protein A complex. Our findings inform the biology and therapeutic opportunities for cohesin-mutant malignancies.

Targeted inactivation of Smc3 or Stag2, and overexpression of mutant cohesin genes in WT mouse and human HSPCs, have been previously studied (12–15), but no cohesin-mutant models currently exist that recapitulate the natural evolution of cohesinmutant myeloid disease in the context of clonal hematopoiesis. Two cohesin complexes are known to co-occur in somatic vertebrate cells, each containing the core components SMC1A, SMC3, and RAD21, and alternatively including STAG2 or the less abundant STAG1 (16). STAG2- and STAG1-containing complexes associate with centromeres and telomeres, respectively, but their sister chromatid cohesion-independent functional differences are not fully understood (1). STAG2 mutations account for over 85% of cohesin mutations in MDS, whereas STAG1 is rarely mutated in MDS or AML (6, 7, 10, 17). The mechanism underlying clonal expansion of these driver mutations is unlikely related to defects in sister chromatid cohesion given lack of association between STAG2 mutations and complex karyotype and aneuploidy (10, 18). STAG1- versus STAG2-containing complexes have been recently shown to differentially contribute to chromatin organization, facilitating longer loops at topologically associating domain (TAD) boundaries and shorter, more transient nested enhancer-promoter contacts, respectively (19–22). Furthermore, deficiency of Stag2 and RUNX family transcription factor 1 (Runx1) has been shown to disrupt enhancer-promoter looping and affect transcriptional pausing leading to selective gene dysregulation (22). We sought to determine the effects of STAG2 mutations observed in patients on the cohesin complex composition and genetic dependencies, with the goal of understanding the mechanisms by which these mutations contribute to cellular transformation and how cohesin-mutant malignancies could be therapeutically targeted.

Results Genetic synthetic vulnerabilities in STAG2-mutant cells. To study the cellular consequences of cohesin mutations in myeloid malignancies, we used CRISPR/Cas9 to engineer a spectrum of predicted LOF STAG2, SMC3, and RAD21 mutations identified in patients in AML cell lines WT for all cohesin subunits and modulators. The different mutants largely phenocopy one another and are consistent with loss of function of STAG2 or haploinsufficiency of SMC3 or RAD21 (Supplemental Figure 1, A–G; supplemental material available online with this article; https://doi.org/10.1172/jci.insight.142149DS1; see Methods). We first focused on STAG2, the most frequently mutated subunit of the cohesin complex, and hypothesized that different STAG2 mutations would be associated with mutant-specific genetic dependencies. We performed genome-scale CRISPR/Cas9 screens in 6 WT and 5 STAG2-mutant U937 cell lines representing different STAG2 mutations using the Avana sgRNA library, which targets a total of 20,000 protein-coding genes with 4 unique sgRNAs per gene and includes 1000 nontargeting sgRNA controls (23). We observed that STAG2-mutant cells were strongly dependent on STAG1, as has been recently reported in the context of bladder cancer and Ewing sarcoma cell lines (24, 25) (Figure 1A and Supplemental Figure 2A). Since both STAG1- and STAG2-containing cohesin complexes participate in sister chromatid cohesion, we examined whether loss of STAG1 in STAG2-deficient cells would lead to aberrant sister chromatid cohesion. We found that loss of both STAG1 and STAG2, but not loss of either one alone, led to sister chromatid cohesion defects as assessed by premature centromere separation and railroad chromosomes (Figure 1B), providing a mechanistic basis for the synthetic lethality of STAG1 and STAG2. The absence of sister chromatid cohesion defects in cells harboring loss of STAG2 alone is in agreement with lack of aneuploidy or complex karyotype in patients with STAG2-mutant MDS and AML (5, 10, 26), as well as previous studies in yeast suggesting that sister chromatid cohesion is unaffected with up to 87% loss of cohesin levels (27). Therefore, STAG2-mutant cells are dependent on the presence of STAG1 and do not have overt sister chromatid cohesion defects unless accompanied by a simultaneous loss of STAG1. In addition to STAG1, we identified preferential dependency of STAG2-mutant cells on multiple components of the DNA damage repair and replication machinery (Figure 1A), as well as lineage-defining transcription factors, and genes involved in mRNA processing (Supplemental Table 1). Of note, we identified multiple members of the base excision repair [poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase 1; PARP1], homologous recombination (BRIP1, RAD51B, RAD51C, RAD54L2, XRCC2, XRCC3, PARP1), mismatch repair (MSH2; DNA polymerase delta 3, accessory subunit [POLD3]; EXO1), and DNA replication (replication protein A2 [RPA2], POLD3) machineries as specific synthetic vulnerabilities of STAG2-mutant cells (Figure 1A). Therefore, we observed differential dependency of STAG2-mutant cells on DNA damage repair and replication-associated pathways.

Altered cohesin complex composition and interactome in STAG2-mutant cells. Having demonstrated that STAG2 mutations lead to genetic dependencies on STAG1 and DNA damage repair and replication, we hypothesized that these cohesin-dependent vulnerabilities could be associated with mutant-specific protein complex alterations. To examine the effect of STAG2 loss on the composition of the cohesin complex, we employed immunoprecipitation using an antibody against the core cohesin ring subunit SMC1A followed by quantitative mass spectrometry (IP-MS) (Supplemental Figure 2B). In WT cells, we detected all members of the cohesin complex, including direct binding partners SMC3 and RAD21, as well as indirect binding partners STAG1, STAG2, and PDS5B (Supplemental Figure 2, C and D; and Supplemental Table 2A). In comparison, examination of STAG2-mutant clones revealed STAG1 to be among the most enriched proteins preferentially incorporated into the cohesin complex in cohesin-mutant cells (hereafter referred to as STAG1-cohesin complex for simplicity) (Figure 1C and Supplemental Table 2B). We validated this switch to STAG1-containing complexes in STAG2-mutant cells using immunoprecipitation followed by Western blotting (Supplemental Figure 2E). A switch from STAG2 to STAG1-cohesin complexes was consistent with the dependency of STAG2-mutant cells on STAG1 (Figure 1A). Unexpectedly, we also observed increased incorporation of STAG1 into cohesin complexes in cells with heterozygous mutation of a non-STAG1/2 paralog cohesin subunit, SMC3 (Supplemental Figure 2, F and G; and Supplemental Table 2C). These studies provide evidence that mutation of either STAG2 or SMC3 causes a shift to STAG1-containing cohesin complexes. We next examined whether the shift from STAG2- to STAG1-containing cohesin complexes is associated with additional changes in its interactome that could explain the genetic dependencies that we had observed. We observed a significant increase in the interaction of the STAG1-cohesin complex with proteins involved in DNA replication and DNA damage repair (e.g., PARP1, RPA1–3; P = 0.024) (Figure 1C), transcription factors, and splicing proteins (Supplemental Table 2B). Similarly, we observed changes in the interaction of the STAG1-cohesin complex with the DNA damage repair, replication, and splicing machinery in SMC3-mutant cells (Supplemental Figure 2F), suggesting that mutations affecting different cohesin subunits may affect the cohesin complex structure and interactome concordantly. These findings demonstrate a high concordance between the cellular processes highlighted by IP-MS experiments and genetic dependency screens in cohesin-mutant cells, especially as it relates to DNA replication and damage repair. Stalled replication forks and accumulation of  dsDNA breaks in STAG2-mutant cells. Having found that STAG2 mutations were associated with a genetic dependency on components of the DNA replication and damage repair pathways, and altered interaction of these proteins with the cohesin complex, we examined whether cells bearing STAG2 mutations accumulate DNA damage. Cohesin has been shown to organize chromatin loops at DNA replication factories in order to mediate replication stress tolerance and restart stalled replication forks (28–32). Since aberrant replication forks could serve as a potential source of DNA damage in cohesin-mutant cells, we investigated DNA replication fork processivity using a DNA fiber assay (33). Loss of STAG2 was associated with an increase in the number of stalled replication forks (6% in WT cells versus 25% in STAG2-mutant cells, P < 0.05) and a tendency to lose replication origin firing (Figure 1D). Furthermore, we observed significant replication fork asymmetry and a 27% decrease in the replication fork rate in STAG2-mutant cells (Supplemental Figure 3, A and B), both of which are consistent with replication fork slowing and stalling. Therefore, STAG2 mutations are associated with abnormal replication fork processivity and stalling, a phenomenon that may be due to aberrant spatial arrangement of replication origins and/ or ineffective restarting of replication forks in the absence of a normal cohesin complex. Stalled replication forks can lead to DNA damage, including dsDNA breaks, if inappropriately resolved. The cohesin complex has been previously implicated in dsDNA break repair and intra-S and G2M checkpoint (34). STAG2-mutant cells are sensitive to PARP inhibition in vitro and in vivo. We next addressed whether altered DNA damage response in STAG2-mutant cells creates a vulnerability that can be exploited therapeutically. In our CRISPR screen for genetic dependencies, we found STAG2-mutant cells to have a genetic dependency on PARP1 (Figure 1A, P = 0.006), and in our IP-MS experiments, we found an increased association of PARP1 with the cohesin complex in STAG2-mutant cells (Figure 1C, log2FC = 1.03). Furthermore, genetic screens in Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Caenorhabditis elegans previously identified synthetic lethality interactions between replication fork mediators, including PARP genes, and mutant cohesin (36). We therefore tested sensitivity of STAG2-mutant cells to PARP inhibition. PARP inhibitors, including talazoparib, inhibit PARP catalytic activity and trap PARP at the sites of DNA damage, rendering cells that are dependent on nonhomologous end joining repair of dsDNA breaks particularly sensitive to these agents. Treatment with talazoparib resulted in approximately 70-fold increased sensitivity of STAG2-mutant cells as compared with WT cells (Figure 2A). In addition, STAG2-mutant cells were outcompeted by WT cells in the presence of talazoparib (Figure 2B). We also sought to determine whether mutations in other components of the cohesin complex result in a similar dependency on PARP inhibition. We found that heterozygous inactivation of SMC3 or RAD21 was associated with increased sensitivity to PARP inhibition to a similar extent as STAG2 mutations in U937 and K562 cells (Figure 2C and Supplemental Figure 3C), suggesting that all core cohesin complex mutations we have tested may act as biomarkers of response to PARP inhibition. We reproduced this effect in xenograft animals injected with individual or competitive mixtures of WT and STAG2-mutant AML cells and observed a genotype-specific effect of talazoparib on STAG2-mutant cells (Figure 2, D and E). Finally, in order to examine whether response to PARP inhibition in primary human leukemia cells is STAG2 mutation dependent, we treated STAG2-mutant and WT primary AML patient samples with talazoparib and noted a dose- and genotype-dependent sensitivity to the drug (Supplemental Figure 3D). STAG2 loss alters chromatin compartmentalization and looping. In order to understand the impact of the aberrant cohesin complex on chromatin compartmentalization and looping, which have been previously linked to DNA replication stress and damage (38), we performed the chromosome conformation analysis Hi-C (39, 40) in a set of STAG2-WT and -knockout AML cell lines. This unbiased genome-wide chromosome conformation analysis enables evaluation of chromatin organization at multiple tiers of genome organization, including compartments, TADs, and loops. Compartments are apparent by the plaid pattern of interaction in Hi-C interaction maps (Figure 5A). Analysis of this pattern is routinely performed by principal component analysis, where principal component 1 (PC1) typically captures the positions of compartment domains. The strength of compartmentalization can then be visualized and quantified by rearranging chromatin interaction maps by ordering loci according to their PC1 value to produce compartmentalization “saddle plots” (41). We observed a global weakening of compartmentalization and spatial segregation of active and inactive chromatin domains in STAG2-knockout cells (Figure 5B), consistent with more intermixing between expression-rich “A compartments” and expression-poor “B compartments” as defined previously (39). Also, the number and location of TAD boundaries, determined by insulation score analysis (42), was largely preserved between STAG2-WT and -mutant cells (Supplemental Figure 5A), but the strength of TAD boundary insulation was globally weakened (Figure 5, C and D; and Supplemental Figure 5B). Finally, we assessed the effects of STAG2 loss on the strength and size distribution of positioned loops that are apparent as dots in Hi-C interaction maps and correspond to enriched CTCF-CTCF (CCCTC binding factor–CCCTC binding factor) interactions at the bases of the loops (43). Visual inspection of the heatmaps revealed stronger dots farther away from the diagonal (arrows in Figure 5E). Genome-wide average loop size and loop density can be estimated by analysis of the relationship between interaction frequency (P) and genomic distance (s) (Supplemental Figure 5C). Specifically, the position of a local maximum in the derivative of P(s) has been previously shown to represent the average loop size (44). In STAG2-WT cells loops were on average 100–200 kb, while in STAG2-knockout cells the average loop size was 200–300 kb. In addition, we noted the loop density to be reduced in STAG2-knockout cells (Figure 5F). Combined, these findings show that in the absence of STAG2, STAG1-containing cohesin complexes extrude larger and somewhat fewer loops. Possibly, STAG1-containing cohesin complexes are blocked less efficiently at CTCF sites (resulting in reduced insulation at CTCF sites and TAD boundaries), allowing the loops to more frequently pass CTCF sites and the formation of larger loops. This longer range extrusion process is also expected to lead to more intermixing of A and B compartments. STAG2 loss leads to increased colocalization of  cohesin with DNA replication and damage repair proteins. A unifying hypothesis for genetic and pharmacologic dependencies on DNA replication and damage response is that altered chromatin insulation and compartment structure in cohesin-mutant cells leads to shifts in the physical colocalization of proteins involved in these cellular processes. We addressed this hypothesis using super-resolution microscopy. Staining for SMC1A protein, we identified WT and mutant cohesin protein complex aggregates as distinct nuclear puncta (Figure 5G). We observed increased colocalization of the STAG1-cohesin complex with PARP1 and RPA1 (Figure 5G). Therefore, we observed STAG2 mutant– dependent alterations in the physical colocalization of the cohesin complex with DNA damage, concordant with our previously identified changes in the cohesin interactome and genetic dependencies. Put in context with our Hi-C analysis, we hypothesize that these changes may be driven by increased processivity of the STAG1-cohesin complex associated with a loss of TAD boundary insulation and longer loop extrusion. These findings are consistent with a model in which cohesin complexes in WT and cohesin-mutant cells, defined by their unique composition, have differential ability to maintain chromatin organization as it relates to spatial organization of DNA damage repair machinery. Decreased colocalization and function of these components in turn creates vulnerabilities that have the potential to be exploited therapeutically in patients with cohesin-mutated malignancies.

Discussion Our studies establish a role for DNA damage, DNA replication, and chromatin architecture in the biology and therapeutic targeting of cohesin-mutant myeloid malignancies. Using genetic screens, IP-MS, chromatin conformation studies, and super-resolution microscopy, we demonstrate that the introduction of cohesin mutations results in a switch from STAG2 to STAG1-cohesin complexes and differential cohesin dependence on DNA damage repair and replication. There are currently very limited therapeutic options for patients with MDS, and no therapies have been identified with selective activity in cohesin-mutant disease. We found that cohesin mutations cause a 70-fold increased sensitivity to PARP inhibition and are a potential biomarker of PARP inhibitor sensitivity in cohesin-mutant myeloid malignancies. PARP inhibitors are currently approved by the FDA for treatment of breast and ovarian cancer in the context of germline BRCA mutations and have been previously tested in a phase I study of unselected patients with advanced hematologic malignancies (45). The effect of talazoparib monotherapy in cohesin-mutated AML or MDS with excess blasts is under investigation in a pilot proof-ofconcept study (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT03974217). STAG2-mutant glioblastoma cells have been previously shown to be sensitive to PARP inhibition in vitro (31, 46), and cohesin mutations may be potential biomarkers of PARP sensitivity in bladder cancer and Ewing sarcoma, where these mutations are common. In addition, combination treatment of hypomethylating agents and PARP inhibition should be considered given sensitivity of cohesin-mutant MDS and genetically engineered CD34+ cells to hypomethylating agents (9, 47), as well as increased sensitivity of PARP inhibition when administered with low-dose hypomethylating agents in preclinical studies (48). Finally, the role of PARP inhibition as a therapeutic strategy may be efficacious in a wider range of myeloid malignancies characterized by DNA damage repair defects, including IDH1/2-AML, FLT3-ITD-AML, splicing factor mutant AML, and AML1-ETO rearranged AML (49). A number of studies have previously examined the effects of complete cohesin loss on chromatin organization, both in the context of an inducible loss of the essential cohesin subunit RAD21 in human cells and loss of the cohesin-loading factor Nipbl in mice (50, 51). These studies confirmed the essential function of the cohesin complex in the formation of topologically associated domains, which is independent of compartment organization. The models used to establish these findings represent a complete loss of cohesin complex, which is not tolerated in human cells and as a result is not implicated in human disease. Patients with cohesin-mutant myeloid malignancies never present with complete, biallelic inactivation of any cohesin subunit, with the notable exception of STAG2, which has a paralog, STAG1. Complete loss of STAG1 and STAG2 was synthetically lethal in our studies as well as in other recent reports (24, 25) and demonstrated in primary mouse HSPCs using Stag2-conditional knockout mice (15). The models used in our study aimed to recapitulate the extent of cohesin dysfunction that would be observed in human disease, using both engineered cell lines as well as primary mouse models of cohesin-mutant MDS and AML. Cohesin mutations are early but usually not initiating lesions in myeloid malignancies. Our in vivo model of cohesin-mutant MDS arising in a setting of Tet2-mutant clones recapitulates the sequential acquisition of cohesin mutations in the context of Tet2-mutant clonal hematopoiesis and the phenotype observed in patients. The approach we developed is highly adaptable and can be used to not only model different stages of disease progression in hematopoietic malignancies but also address the question of order of mutation acquisition and questions of necessity versus sufficiency for transformation using different genetic combinations. Cohesin has been previously shown to organize chromatin loops at DNA replication factories into rosette-like structures, which allows for organized firing of multiple origins of replication and is disrupted with lower levels of cohesin leading to longer loop formation, similar to our observations with STAG2- versus STAG1-cohesin complexes (38). # BCL11B Drives Human Mammary Stem Cell Self-Renewal In Vitro by Inhibiting Basal Differentiation

**Authors:** Daniel H Miller; Dexter X Jin; Ethan S Sokol; Janel R Cabrera; Daphne A Superville; Rebecca A Gorelov; Charlotte Kuperwasser; Piyush B Gupta

**Affiliations:** 1Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research, 455 Main St., Cambridge, MA 02142, USA | 2Department of Biology, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA 02139, USA | 3Department of Developmental, Chemical, and Molecular Biology, Tufts University School of Medicine, 136 Harrison Avenue, Boston, MA 02111, USA | 4Raymond & Beverly Sackler Convergence Laboratory, Tufts University School of Medicine, 145 Harrison Avenue, Boston, MA 02111, USA | 5Department of Biology, Williams College, Williamstown, MA 01267, USA | 6Koch Institute for Integrative Cancer Research at MIT, Cambridge, MA 02139, USA | 7Harvard Stem Cell Institute, Cambridge, MA 02138, USA

## Abstract

The epithelial compartment of the mammary gland contains basal and luminal cell lineages, as well as stem and progenitor cells that reside upstream in the differentiation hierarchy. Stem and progenitor cell differentiation is regulated to maintain adult tissue and mediate expansion during pregnancy and lactation. The genetic factors that regulate the transition of cells between differentiation states remain incompletely understood. Here, we present a genome-scale method to discover genes driving cell-state specification. Applying this method, we identify a transcription factor, BCL11B, which drives stem cell self-renewal in vitro, by inhibiting differentiation into the basal lineage. To validate BCL11B's functional role, we use two-dimensional colony-forming and three-dimensional tissue differentiation assays to assess the lineage differentiation potential and functional abilities of primary human mammary cells. These findings show that BCL11B regulates mammary cell differentiation and demonstrate the utility of our proposed genome-scale strategy for identifying lineage regulators in mammalian tissues.

Keywords: human mammary gland biology, mammary epithelial stem cells, BCL11B, epigenetics, single-cell genomics, epithelial differentiation, three-dimensional cell culture
